topics.title: How Oxygen Gets From the Air to the Cells
topics.summary: Oxygen reaches the cells only when air moves in (ventilation), gas crosses the alveoli (diffusion), and blood carries it away (perfusion).
objectives: You can explain oxygenation, ventilation, and respiration in your own words.
You can trace air from the nose to the alveoli and say what each part does.
You can explain why rising CO₂ speeds up breathing and low CO₂ slows it.
You can tell an airflow problem from a blood-flow problem (V/Q mismatch).
You can tell hypoxemia from hypoxia and give normal breathing rates by age.
topics.bigPicture:
Every cell in the body needs oxygen to make energy. Oxygenation means getting oxygen to all of those cells. The lungs do this job together with the heart and blood.

Almost every oxygenation problem comes down to one of three breakdowns. Air can't get in. Air gets in but can't cross into the blood. Or blood can't reach the air. If you can name which one is broken, you can predict what you will see and what to do.
recap: Oxygenation = oxygen to every cell. Ventilation = air in and out. Respiration = gas exchange.
The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and straighter, so aspiration goes right, and down to the lower lobe when upright.
Cartilage holds the trachea and bronchi open. Smooth muscle around the bronchioles can tighten in bronchospasm.
Negative pressure in the pleural space keeps the lung expanded. Air in that space collapses the lung.
Gas exchange needs both open, air-filled alveoli and good blood flow. A mismatch (V/Q mismatch) causes hypoxemia.
CO₂, through H⁺, is the main signal to breathe. High CO₂ speeds breathing; low CO₂ slows it.
Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood. Untreated, it leads to hypoxia, low oxygen in the tissues.
SpO₂ can look normal when hemoglobin is low. Full trucks, but too few of them.

keyTerms.def: The process of getting oxygen to all cells of the body.
Moving air into the lungs (inhalation, or inspiration) and out of the lungs (exhalation, or expiration).
The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide at the cell level. People often use the word loosely to mean breathing.
Normal, effortless breathing at the expected rate for the person's age.
Tiny hair-like projections lining the airways. They beat in waves to sweep mucus and particles up and out.
Tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the end of the airways where gas exchange happens.
Sudden tightening of the smooth muscle around the bronchioles, which narrows the airway, as in an asthma attack.
The two-layer lining around each lung. The visceral layer covers the lung. The parietal layer lines the chest wall. The pleural space lies between.
Air in the pleural space. The negative pressure is lost, and the lung collapses.
Blood flow through tissue. In the lungs, blood flowing past the alveoli to pick up oxygen.
How well ventilation (V, air reaching the alveoli) matches perfusion (Q, blood reaching the alveoli).
Collapse of alveoli, often from shallow breathing or a blocked airway.
The protein in red blood cells that carries most of the oxygen in the blood.
A low level of oxygen in the blood. The ending "-emia" means blood.
Low oxygen delivery to the tissues. Untreated hypoxemia leads to hypoxia.

sections.heading: What is oxygenation?
sections.keyIdea: Oxygenation is the goal; ventilation moves the air; respiration trades the gases.
sections.body:
Three words sound alike but mean different things. Oxygenation is the big goal: oxygen delivered to every cell. Ventilation is the mechanical part. It moves air in (inspiration) and out (expiration).

Respiration is the chemical part. Oxygen and carbon dioxide (CO₂) trade places at the cell level. People often say "respiration" when they really mean ventilation.

Breathing is normally autonomic. That means it happens on its own, without thinking. So any change in breathing pattern needs attention right away. If something this automatic has changed, something in the body has changed.

check.q: A client's respiratory rate is normal, but the cells are still not getting enough oxygen. Is that possible?
check.a: Yes. Air can move normally while gas exchange or blood flow fails. Examples are a clot blocking blood flow in the lung, or too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen.

sections.heading: How does the nose prepare the air?
sections.keyIdea: The nose warms, moistens, and filters air; cilia and sneezing sweep irritants out.
sections.body:
The upper airway is the inlet for air. The nose is normally the main entry point. As air passes through the nares (nostrils), it is warmed, humidified (moistened), and filtered.

The upper airway also protects the lungs. Sneezing blows irritants out of the nose. Cilia beat in waves to sweep mucus and trapped particles up and out. Then the person coughs them out or swallows them.

People can also breathe through the mouth. Mouth breathing still gets air into the lungs. But it skips most of the warming, moistening, and filtering.
bullets: Smoking damages cilia, so mucus is not cleared well.
Mucus pools overnight. That is why a smoker often coughs it up in the morning.
sections.analogy: Think of the nose as the body's air conditioner. It heats, moistens, and filters the air before it reaches the delicate lungs.

sections.heading: The lower airway: trachea to alveoli
sections.keyIdea: The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and straighter, so aspirated material usually goes to the right lower lobe.
sections.body:
The trachea (windpipe) is the entrance to the lungs. In healthy breathing at rest, the neck muscles stay relaxed. The chest rises and falls evenly on both sides. Breathing out takes about twice as long as breathing in.

Tight, working neck muscles are not normal. Neither is one side of the chest moving less than the other.

At its lower end, the trachea splits into the right and left bronchi. The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and straighter. So when a person aspirates (breathes in) food, vomit, or an object, it usually goes right. In an upright client, gravity pulls it into the right lower lobe.
bullets: Trachea and bronchi: held open by stiff rings of cartilage, so they don't collapse.
Bronchioles: wrapped in smooth muscle, which can tighten (bronchospasm). That is why bronchodilator medicines target the bronchioles.
Bronchioles lead to alveolar ducts, then alveolar sacs, made of single alveoli, where gas exchange happens.
sections.example: An 84-year-old with GERD and a weak cough chokes on lunch while sitting up in a chair. Where do you listen most closely? Over the right lower lobe. The right bronchus is straighter, and gravity pulls material down. If a client seems to aspirate during a tube feeding, stop the feeding and sit the client up first.

sections.heading: Lungs, lobes, and the pleura
sections.keyIdea: Negative pressure in the pleural space holds the lung open; air in that space makes the lung collapse.
sections.body:
The right lung has 3 lobes: upper, middle, and lower. The left lung has 2 lobes: upper and lower. The lower lobes are the largest.

Each lung is wrapped in pleura, a lining with two layers. The visceral pleura covers the lung. The parietal pleura lines the inside of the chest wall. The pleural space lies between them. The pleura helps breathing and keeps the lungs separate.

The pressure in the pleural space is normally negative. That means it is lower than the air pressure outside. This slight suction holds the lung against the chest wall. When the chest expands, the lung expands with it.

If air gets into the pleural space, that suction is lost. The lung collapses. This is a pneumothorax.
sections.analogy: The two pleural layers are like two panes of wet glass stuck together. They slide easily but are hard to pull apart. Let air between them, and they separate.

check.q: How many lobes does each lung have, and which are largest?
check.a: Right lung 3, left lung 2. The lower (inferior) lobes are the largest.

sections.heading: What happens inside the alveoli?
sections.keyIdea: Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the blood, CO₂ moves out, and hemoglobin carries the oxygen away.
sections.body:
Each alveolus is a tiny sac with a wall only one cell thick. It is wrapped in a net of tiny blood vessels called capillaries. Gas moves from where there is a lot to where there is little. This is called diffusion.

Air in the alveolus has lots of oxygen. Blood arriving from the body has little. So oxygen moves into the blood. That blood carries lots of CO₂, so CO₂ moves into the alveolus and is breathed out.

Once in the blood, most oxygen rides on hemoglobin inside red blood cells. If hemoglobin is low, as in severe anemia or bleeding, the blood can't carry enough oxygen. This is true even when each hemoglobin is fully loaded.

So the lungs deliver oxygen well only when two things work. The alveoli must be open and full of air. The capillaries must have good blood flow.
sections.example: A client with a slow GI bleed has hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL. The client is tired and short of breath walking to the bathroom. HR 118, RR 24, SpO₂ 98%. How? SpO₂ only shows the percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. The few trucks are full, but there are too few trucks. Tissues are hypoxic despite a normal SpO₂.

sections.heading: What is a V/Q mismatch?
sections.keyIdea: Air and blood must meet at the same alveolus; if either is blocked, blood leaves the lungs low on oxygen.
sections.body:
For gas exchange to work, air (V) and blood (Q) must meet at the same alveolus. The V/Q ratio describes how well they match.

When they don't match, blood leaves the lungs without enough oxygen. The cells of the body then don't get enough oxygen. There are two ways this happens.

table.caption: Two kinds of V/Q mismatch
rows: Sputum, inflammation, atelectasis, fluid volume excess
Blood flows past, but no fresh air is there to give it oxygen.
Blood clots, plaque buildup, emphysematous (damaged, overstretched) alveoli
Fresh air sits in the alveolus, but little blood comes by to pick it up.

sections.example: Three days after knee surgery, a client says, "Something is wrong." RR 30, HR 124, SpO₂ 88% on room air. Lungs are clear, and the chest rises evenly. Air is moving fine, so think blood flow: a clot may be blocking the lung. Stay with the client, raise the head of the bed, give oxygen per protocol, and call the provider now.

check.q: Is pneumonia with fluid-filled alveoli an airflow or a blood-flow problem?
check.a: Airflow. Fluid and inflammation keep fresh air out of the alveoli, even though blood still flows past. Lung-expansion care helps airflow problems. Anticoagulants treat clot (blood-flow) problems.

sections.heading: What controls how fast we breathe?
sections.keyIdea: CO₂ is the main signal to breathe: more CO₂ means faster, deeper breaths; less CO₂ means slower breaths.
sections.body:
The drive to breathe mainly responds to hydrogen ions (H⁺) in arterial blood. H⁺ is what makes blood acidic. CO₂ mixes with water to form an acid. So when CO₂ goes up, H⁺ goes up too.

In plain words, CO₂ is the main signal to breathe.

Always judge a breathing rate against the client's age. A rate of 44 is normal for a 6-month-old but alarming in an adult. Count an infant's or young child's breathing for a full 60 seconds, because it is often irregular.
steps: CO₂ rises (exercise, or slow breathing). H⁺ rises, and pH falls (more acidic).
The brain senses this and makes breathing faster and deeper.
Faster, deeper breaths blow off CO₂. H⁺ falls, and pH returns toward normal.
The reverse: CO₂ falls (after hyperventilating). pH rises. The drive to breathe drops, and breathing slows until CO₂ builds back up.
sections.example: A client hyperventilated during a panic attack. The ABG showed pH 7.50 and PaCO₂ 29. Now calm, the client breathes 10 times a minute with brief pauses, SpO₂ 97%, alert. Tell the spouse: "Fast breathing lowered the carbon dioxide, the body's main signal to breathe. As it builds back up, breathing will return to normal." Keep watching the rate, alertness, and SpO₂.

sections.heading: Hypoxemia vs. hypoxia: what is the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood; left untreated, it becomes hypoxia, low oxygen in the tissues.
sections.body:
Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood. You find it with numbers like PaO₂ and SaO₂. If it is not treated, it leads to hypoxia, which means low oxygen delivery to the tissues.

You see hypoxia in the client's brain, energy, and behavior. Mild oxygen problems cause vague signs that are easy to brush off: fatigue, irritability, and discomfort. Severe problems can be fatal. So take small changes seriously.

Oxygenation links to other concepts: acid–base balance, cellular regulation, cognition, comfort, perfusion, and stress and coping. Low oxygen clouds thinking. Breathlessness feeds anxiety.
sections.example: A client with pneumonia is irritable and very tired. ABG: pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 36, PaO₂ 58, SaO₂ 89%. The pH and CO₂ are normal, but oxygen is low. That is hypoxemia. The irritability and fatigue show the brain is not getting enough. Hypoxia is developing. Normal pH and CO₂ do not mean normal oxygen.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most mistakes come from mixing up look-alike words or trusting a normal-looking number.
sections.body: These pairs trip students up. Learn the one fact that tells them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Hypoxemia = low O₂ in the blood (a lab number). Hypoxia = low O₂ in the tissues (restless, confused, tired).
Ventilation moves air. Respiration exchanges gases at the cell level.
Crackles, diminished sounds, or sputum point to airflow. Sudden low O₂ with clear lungs points to blood flow (a clot).
SpO₂ is a percent. With low hemoglobin it can read 98% while the tissues starve.
Right is shorter, wider, straighter. Upright client: right lower lobe.
Cartilage (trachea, bronchi) stays open. Smooth muscle (bronchioles) can spasm.
Low CO₂ weakens the drive to breathe. Slow breathing for a short time is expected; keep monitoring.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Questions give you a bedside picture and ask you to find which step of oxygenation is broken.
sections.body: Expect these patterns. Each tests whether you can apply anatomy and physiology, not just recite it.
bullets: Where will the aspiration go? (right lower lobe if upright)
Clear lungs but sudden low SpO₂ after surgery or immobility (think clot)
Normal SpO₂ but tired, fast heart rate, low hemoglobin (think anemia)
Why breathing slowed after hyperventilation (low CO₂)
Is this respiratory rate normal for this age?
steps: Read the stem: "A client 3 days after hip surgery suddenly has RR 30, HR 124, SpO₂ 88%. Lungs are clear and chest rise is equal. What does the nurse suspect?"
What is it really asking? Which part of oxygenation is broken: airflow or blood flow?
Key cues: sudden onset, recent surgery and immobility, clear and equal breath sounds.
Wrong: "pneumonia" needs crackles or fever. "Atelectasis" gives diminished sounds at the bases. "Anxiety" ignores the low SpO₂.
Answer: a blood clot blocking blood flow in the lung (a perfusion problem). Stay, give oxygen per protocol, call the provider.
Strategy: when SpO₂ drops, ask "Can air get in? Can gas cross? Can blood reach it?" The normal findings point to the broken part.

sections.heading: Worked case: the quiet post-op client
sections.keyIdea: Pain causes shallow breathing, shallow breathing causes atelectasis, and atelectasis blocks airflow.
sections.body: A client is 1 day after abdominal surgery. The client holds the belly and takes shallow breaths. Breath sounds are diminished at both bases. SpO₂ has drifted from 96% to 91%. The client seems a little irritable.
steps: Notice: shallow breaths, diminished sounds at the bases, falling SpO₂, new irritability.
Ask: is this airflow or blood flow? Diminished sounds mean air is not reaching the alveoli. This is an airflow problem.
Name it: pain led to shallow breathing, and alveoli collapsed (atelectasis).
Act: treat the pain first so the client can breathe deeply. Then coach deep breathing, incentive spirometry, splinted coughing, and walking.
Evaluate: SpO₂ back near baseline, clearer breath sounds, calmer behavior.

check.q: Why treat the pain before coaching the incentive spirometer?
check.a: Pain is the reason the client won't breathe deeply. Until the pain is controlled, the client can't take the deep breaths that reopen the alveoli.

mnemonics.name: Air in, across, away
mnemonics.text: Air must get IN (ventilation), go ACROSS the alveoli (diffusion), and be carried AWAY by blood (perfusion). Find the broken step.

pearls: Aspiration goes right, and down to the lower lobe when the client is upright.
Bronchioles have smooth muscle, not cartilage, so they can spasm. That is where bronchodilators work.
Sudden hypoxemia with clear, equal lungs points to a blood-flow problem such as a clot.
Low CO₂ after hyperventilation slows breathing; high CO₂ speeds it up.
A normal SpO₂ does not rule out hypoxia when hemoglobin is low. Judge anemia by tolerance of activity, not SpO₂.
Normal pH and CO₂ do not mean normal oxygenation. Always read the PaO₂ and SaO₂.
redFlags: Drowsy post-anesthesia client with snoring breaths, retractions, and falling SpO₂: the airway is blocked. Open it first (reposition head and jaw), then reassess.
Sudden shortness of breath, fast heart rate, and low SpO₂ with clear lungs after surgery or bed rest: stay, give oxygen per protocol, call the provider now.
Coughing or choking during a tube feeding: stop the feeding and sit the client up.
New irritability or fatigue with a falling SpO₂: treat it as an oxygen problem until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Why do bronchodilators work on the bronchioles and not the trachea?
checks.a: Bronchioles are wrapped in smooth muscle that can tighten or relax. The trachea is held open by stiff cartilage.

checks.q: Air leaks into the pleural space. What happens to the lung, and why?
checks.a: It collapses, because the negative pressure that held it against the chest wall is lost.

checks.q: A client with severe anemia has SpO₂ 99% and asks, "Why can't I breathe if my oxygen is fine?" How do you explain it?
checks.a: "Your red cells are full of oxygen, but you have fewer of them than normal. Less oxygen reaches your body, so your heart and lungs work harder to make up for it."

checks.q: A client with heart failure has fluid in the alveoli. Is this an airflow or blood-flow problem, and what helps first?
checks.a: Airflow. Fluid volume excess blocks air from the alveoli. Sit the client upright, give oxygen as ordered, and notify the provider.

checks.q: A 6-month-old breathes 44 times a minute. Normal?
checks.a: Yes. Infants normally breathe 30–60 times a minute. Count for a full 60 seconds before deciding.

topics.title: Respiratory Assessment and Signs of Hypoxia
topics.summary: Before any monitor beeps, your eyes, ears, hands, and questions can tell you whether a client is getting enough oxygen.
objectives: You can spot early and late signs of hypoxia and explain why behavior changes first.
You can take a focused respiratory history, including cough, sputum, pain, risks, and medicines.
You can read posture, effort, color, and voice for signs of distress.
You can name the three normal breath sounds and where each belongs.
You can link stridor, crackles, rhonchi, wheezes, and friction rub to their causes.
You can decide which respiratory findings need RN action right now.
topics.bigPicture:
A pulse oximeter gives you one number. A good assessment gives you the whole story. Low oxygen often shows up first as a change in behavior, like restlessness or confusion. That happens long before a client turns blue.

Assessment combines subjective data (what the client tells you) and objective data (what you see, hear, feel, and measure). In the M.L. case, the nurse knew M.L. was in trouble before any test came back. She spoke only a few words at a time, leaned forward on her knees, sounded hoarse, and breathed 32 times a minute.
recap: The brain signals low oxygen first: restlessness, irritability, sudden confusion, plus a faster heart rate and breathing rate.
Early hypoxia is restless and fast. Late hypoxia is blue, slow, and low (cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension).
Tripod posture and speaking only 1–3 words mean severe distress, whatever the SpO₂ says.
Bronchial = trachea. Bronchovesicular = beside sternum and between scapulae. Vesicular = lung fields and bases. Right sound, wrong place = abnormal.
Stridor = upper airway emergency. Crackles = fluid or collapsed alveoli. Rhonchi = secretions. Wheezes = narrow airways. Friction rub = inflamed pleura.
Consolidation: dull, more fremitus, bronchial sounds. Air (pneumothorax): hyperresonant, less fremitus, less chest rise.
A quiet chest in a client who was wheezing is getting worse, not better.
Treat the client, not the number. Assess new restlessness before giving any sedative.

keyTerms.def: What the client reports, such as shortness of breath or chest pain.
What the nurse sees or measures, such as respiratory rate, SpO₂, or breath sounds.
Listening to body sounds with a stethoscope.
Extra or abnormal lung sounds: crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, stridor, or a friction rub.
Sitting and leaning forward with hands on the knees or a table. A sign of serious breathing distress.
Extra muscles, such as those in the neck, used to breathe when normal effort is not enough.
Skin pulling in between the ribs, below the ribs, or above the sternum when breathing in. A sign of extra effort.
Bluish color of the skin, lips, or nail beds from low oxygen. It is a late sign.
Rounded, enlarged fingertips and nail beds from long-term low oxygen, as in COPD.
Vibration you feel on the chest as the client speaks. Stronger over solid lung, weaker over air.
Lung tissue that has turned solid because the alveoli are filled with fluid or pus, as in pneumonia.
A crackling, "crispy rice" feel under the skin from air trapped in the tissues.
A loud, high-pitched crowing sound when breathing in. It means the upper airway is narrowing. An emergency.
Trouble breathing when lying flat, relieved by sitting up.
A measure of smoking history: packs smoked per day times the number of years smoked.

sections.heading: Why does behavior change first?
sections.keyIdea: The brain has almost no oxygen reserve, so new restlessness or confusion is often the first sign of hypoxia.
sections.body:
The brain uses a lot of oxygen and stores almost none. When oxygen drops, the brain is one of the first organs to complain. So the early signs of hypoxia are often behavior changes.

At first the body fights back. The heart beats faster and breathing speeds up to deliver more oxygen. This is called compensation. Later, the body runs out of ways to cope. Then the heart slows and blood pressure falls.
bullets: Increasing restlessness and irritability
Sudden, unexplained confusion
Fast heart rate plus fast breathing rate

table.caption: Early vs. late signs of hypoxia
rows: Confusion worsening to stupor or no response

sections.example: Two days after abdominal surgery, a client is restless, pulling at the gown, and says, "I just feel really anxious." HR 112, RR 26. The client asks for PRN lorazepam. New "anxiety" with a fast pulse and fast breathing is hypoxia until proven otherwise. Check SpO₂ and lungs first. A sedative could slow breathing and hide the warning signs.

check.q: Why is bradycardia in a hypoxic client more worrying than tachycardia?
check.a: Tachycardia means the body is still coping. Bradycardia means the heart itself is running out of oxygen. See this client first.

sections.heading: What do you ask in the history?
sections.keyIdea: The history tells you the client's baseline and risks, so you can spot what is new.
sections.body: Each history question has a purpose. Here is what to ask and why. Remember M.L.: asthma since childhood, a recent bout of bronchitis, and a rescue inhaler used four times a day.
bullets: Current breathing problems and past lung disease: asthma, COPD, recent bronchitis or pneumonia. This sets the baseline.
Lifestyle: activity level, work and home setting, exposure to smoke, dust, or chemicals.
Cough and sputum: when it happens, dry or productive, and the sputum's color, amount, and thickness. Thick mucus can block airways. A color change can mean infection.
Chest pain: where it is, and whether breathing or coughing makes it worse (pleuritic pain).
Risk factors: smoking and secondhand smoke, irritants, recent illness, immobility, surgery. Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked.
Medicines: how often the rescue inhaler is used, plus opioids and sedatives, which slow breathing.
Sleep: trouble breathing lying flat (orthopnea). Ask how many pillows the client needs.

check.q: A client smoked 2 packs a day for 15 years. How many pack-years?
check.a: 30 pack-years (2 × 15). Use years smoked, not the client's age.

sections.heading: What can you see before you touch?
sections.keyIdea: Posture, speech, voice, effort, and color can reveal severe distress before any test does.
sections.body: Much of the exam is just looking carefully. Watch how the client sits, talks, and works to breathe. Long-standing findings like clubbing or a barrel chest are part of the baseline. New findings like restlessness or stridor are the urgent ones.

table.caption: What you see and what it means
rows: Posture: sitting up, leaning forward, hands on knees (tripod)
The client is using position to help the chest expand. Severe distress.
Severe distress. Full sentences mean more air is moving.
Normal breathing muscles are not enough.
That lung is not expanding (collapse, or air in the pleural space).
Cyanosis is late. In darker skin, check lips, tongue, inside the mouth, and conjunctivae.
Long-term low oxygen, such as COPD.
Chronic air trapping, or spine curves that limit lung expansion.

sections.example: M.L., 30, with asthma, sits leaning forward, hands on her knees. She speaks a few words at a time. Her voice is hoarse, her face pale. RR 32, SpO₂ 91% on room air, breath sounds decreased. Every finding points to severe distress. The nurse reports right away, and the provider starts oxygen at 4 L/min by nasal cannula.

sections.heading: What do your hands tell you?
sections.keyIdea: Solid lung makes vibration stronger and sounds dull; extra air makes vibration weaker and sounds hollow.
sections.body:
Place your hands on the back of the chest with thumbs near the spine. Ask the client to breathe deeply. Your thumbs should move apart equally. The side that moves less has the problem.

Tactile fremitus is the vibration you feel when the client says "ninety-nine." Sound travels better through solid or fluid than through air. So fremitus is stronger over consolidation, as in pneumonia. It is weaker over extra air, as in a pneumothorax.

Percussion (tapping) over solid lung sounds dull. Over trapped air it sounds hyperresonant, or extra hollow. Crepitus is never expected. Find its source. Spreading crepitus with a voice change can threaten the airway.

table.caption: Solid lung vs. extra air
rows: Bronchial sounds in the lung field

sections.analogy: Fremitus is like feeling music through a wall. Through a solid wall, you feel the bass strongly. Through an empty room full of air, the vibration fades.

sections.heading: What do normal breath sounds sound like?
sections.keyIdea: Each normal breath sound belongs in one place; a normal sound in the wrong place is abnormal.
sections.body: Normal lungs make three kinds of sounds. Each belongs in a certain spot. Listen on bare skin with the diaphragm of the stethoscope. Compare side to side. Listen through a full breath in and out at each spot.

table.caption: Normal breath sounds
rows: Beside the sternum and between the scapulae
Lung fields, loudest at the bases

sections.example: A client has right lower lobe pneumonia. Over that lobe you hear loud, high-pitched bronchial sounds. You also feel more fremitus and percuss dullness. Bronchial sounds belong over the trachea, not the lung base. The solid lung is carrying tracheal sounds to the surface.

check.q: You hear soft, low-pitched sounds over the lung bases, longer on breathing in. Normal?
check.a: Yes. Those are vesicular sounds in their normal place.

sections.heading: Which abnormal sounds should worry you?
sections.keyIdea: Stridor is an emergency; the other sounds point you to fluid, mucus, narrow airways, or inflamed pleura.
sections.body:
There are five adventitious sounds to know. Each points to a different problem. If you hear one, ask the client to cough and listen again. Some clear with coughing; most don't.

Stridor can appear after the breathing tube is removed (extubation) or after neck surgery. New noisy breathing in with a hoarse voice may be stridor. Assess right away.

table.caption: Adventitious breath sounds
rows: Loud, high crowing when breathing in; often heard without a stethoscope
Upper airway narrowing: swelling or an object
Short pops, like hair rubbed near your ear; often on breathing in
Fluid in alveoli or collapsed alveoli popping open: pneumonia, atelectasis, fluid overload
Low snoring or gurgling, often on breathing out
High musical whistle, often on breathing out
Narrow small airways: asthma, COPD, bronchospasm
Grating, like leather rubbing; in and out; one spot
Inflamed pleura rubbing; sharp pain with breathing

sections.example: A client with chronic bronchitis has a loud, low snoring sound over the large airways when breathing out. After a strong cough, the sound changes. These are rhonchi: mucus that moves with coughing. Encourage coughing and deep breathing to clear it.

check.q: Which sound means you call for help right away, and why?
check.a: Stridor. The upper airway is narrowing and could close completely.

sections.heading: How do you decide who needs you now?
sections.keyIdea: Go first to new or worsening signs of hypoxia, and always match the number to the client.
sections.body:
Assessment matters only if you act on it. Assistive personnel (AP) may take vital signs and give basic care to stable clients. The RN assesses, interprets, teaches, and evaluates.

When an AP reports a number, ask three things. Is it new? Is it getting worse? Does it fit the other clues? Judge each number against the client's age, baseline, and prescribed target.
steps: Airway: can the client speak? Any stridor, snoring, or gurgling?
Breathing: rate, depth, effort, posture, chest symmetry, full sentences?
SpO₂: compare with baseline, and match it to how the client looks.
Mental status: new restlessness, irritability, or confusion?
Listen to all lung fields side to side. Note abnormal or absent sounds.
Act: sit the client up, give oxygen as ordered, and call the provider for new or worse findings.
sections.example: An AP reports four clients. One is alert with SpO₂ 95%. One is newly restless and trying to climb out of bed. One speaks in 2–3 word phrases. One had SpO₂ 89% that did not improve after sitting up. The RN goes now to the last three. New restlessness, short phrases, and low oxygen that won't improve are all signs of hypoxia.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Quiet does not mean better, and a calm number does not cancel a struggling client.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause the most missed questions. Use the right column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Wheezing that fades while the client gets drowsy means little air is moving. Escalate now.
New "anxiety" with fast HR and RR is hypoxia until proven otherwise. Assess before sedating.
Rhonchi often clear or change with coughing. Crackles usually do not.
Stridor: loud, on breathing in, upper airway, emergency. Wheeze: musical, usually breathing out, small airways.
Rub: grating, one spot, in and out, painful breathing. Crackles: pops, often at the bases.
Clubbing and barrel chest are baseline. New restlessness, rising HR, or stridor are acute.
Cyanosis is late and hard to see in darker skin. Do not wait for it.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect priority questions that hide early hypoxia behind normal-looking numbers or "anxiety."
sections.body: Common patterns you will see:
bullets: Which client to see first (new signs of hypoxia, late signs, stridor)
Early vs. late hypoxia from a set of vital signs
Matching a breath sound to its cause or location
A client asking for a sedative while restless
Which task you can give to an AP
steps: Read the stem: "An asthma client was wheezing loudly an hour ago. Now breath sounds are faint, and the client is drowsy. SpO₂ 90%. What is the nurse's best action?"
What is it really asking? Is this client better or worse?
Key cues: wheezing has faded, drowsiness is new, SpO₂ is borderline.
Wrong: "document improvement" misreads the silent chest. "Let the client rest" ignores drowsiness. "Recheck in 1 hour" delays care.
Answer: call for help right away (rapid response) and support breathing. Very little air is moving, and CO₂ may be rising.
Strategy: when a symptom disappears, ask "Did the problem fix itself, or did the client stop fighting?" Check level of consciousness.

sections.heading: Worked case: M.L. in the clinic
sections.keyIdea: Put posture, speech, voice, rate, and sounds together to judge how sick a client is.
sections.body: M.L., 30, has asthma and recent bronchitis. She woke at night unable to get enough air and propped herself on 3 pillows. Now she leans forward on the exam table. She speaks a few words at a time. RR 32, SpO₂ 91%, decreased breath sounds.
steps: Notice: tripod posture, short phrases, hoarse voice, RR 32, SpO₂ 91%, decreased sounds.
Cluster the cues: these all point to severe distress, not mild asthma.
History clues: orthopnea and a rescue inhaler used four times a day show poor control.
Act: sit her upright, give oxygen as ordered, stay with her, and report to the provider now.
Evaluate: longer sentences, slower rate, better SpO₂, and clearer breath sounds.

check.q: What term describes M.L.'s trouble breathing when lying flat, and how do you track it?
check.a: Orthopnea. Ask how many pillows she needs to sleep and document it. More pillows means things are getting worse.

pearls: Restlessness in a post-op client is hypoxia until proven otherwise. Assess oxygen before giving a sedative.
Early hypoxia = restless and fast. Late hypoxia = blue, slow, and low.
Speaking only a few words at a time is severe distress, whatever the oximeter says.
Right sound, wrong place = abnormal. Bronchial sounds over a lung base suggest consolidation.
Have the client cough and listen again. Rhonchi often clear; crackles and wheezes usually don't.
Check for cyanosis inside the mouth and in the conjunctivae in clients with darker skin.
redFlags: Stridor, including after extubation or neck surgery: stay with the client, call for help, prepare to support the airway.
New confusion or agitation with fast breathing: check SpO₂ and airway, give oxygen as ordered, call the provider.
Speaking 1–3 words, tripod position, neck muscles working: sit upright, give oxygen as ordered, get help.
Wheezing that fades to faint or absent sounds with drowsiness: airflow is failing; escalate now.
Central cyanosis, bradycardia, or hypotension in a hypoxic client: late signs; call a rapid response.

checks.q: After surgery, HR rises from 84 to 110, RR from 16 to 24, BP is slightly up, and the client is newly irritable. Early or late hypoxia?
checks.a: Early. The body is still coping with a faster heart and breathing rate. Act now, before late signs appear.

checks.q: Where do you expect bronchovesicular sounds, and what is their timing?
checks.a: Beside the sternum and between the scapulae. Breathing in and out are equal in length.

checks.q: A client has a grating sound in one spot, in and out, and says it hurts to breathe deeply. What is it?
checks.a: A pleural friction rub: inflamed pleural layers rubbing together.

checks.q: One side of the chest rises less. Fremitus is decreased and breath sounds are faint on that side. What do you suspect?
checks.a: Air in the pleural space (pneumothorax). Report it right away.

checks.q: Why ask how often a client uses a rescue inhaler?
checks.a: Frequent use, like four times a day, shows poor control. The client may be heading for a serious attack.

checks.q: Can the AP decide whether a client's new restlessness is serious?
checks.a: No. The AP can measure and report. The RN must assess and interpret the change.

topics.title: Breathing Patterns and Changes in Oxygenation
topics.summary: Rate, depth, and rhythm are clues. Read the breathing pattern, and it points you to the problem, from a blocked airway to acidosis to a failing brain.
objectives: You can sort a breathing problem into gas exchange, airway patency, or breathing pattern.
You can explain how COPD, secretions, inflammation, and atelectasis interfere with oxygenation.
You can define tachypnea, bradypnea, hyperventilation, hypoventilation, apnea, dyspnea, and orthopnea.
You can recognize Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, and Biot breathing and their causes.
You can choose independent nursing actions that improve breathing.
topics.bigPicture:
Breathing is automatic. The body quietly adjusts each breath to keep oxygen up and CO₂ balanced. So when the pattern changes, the body is telling you something is wrong. A change in breathing pattern needs attention right away.

Some patterns are the body helping itself, like deep, fast breathing to blow off acid. Others are signs of failure, like slow breathing from too much opioid. Your job is to describe the pattern, find what is driving it, and act.
recap: Describe problems by gas exchange (can gas cross?), airway patency (is the tube open?), and pattern (rate, depth, rhythm).
COPD damages alveoli: CO₂ builds up, O₂ stays low. Look for retractions, cyanosis, and clubbing.
Airway obstruction is the main cause of atelectasis. Pain and shallow breathing after surgery set it up.
Tachypnea is over 20/min; bradypnea is under 10/min (per your slides). Apnea is no breathing.
Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ (alkalosis, tingling). Hypoventilation keeps CO₂ (acidosis, drowsiness).
Kussmaul = metabolic acidosis. Cheyne-Stokes = heart failure, high ICP, overdose. Biot = CNS disorders.
Positioning, deep breathing, pursed-lip breathing, pacing, and secretion clearance are independent. Changing oxygen flow needs an order.

keyTerms.def: How open and clear the airway is.
Breathing too fast: over 20 breaths a minute in an adult (per your slides).
Breathing too slow: under 10 breaths a minute (per your slides).
Fast, deep breathing that blows off too much CO₂.
Breathing too slow or shallow, so too little oxygen reaches the lungs and CO₂ builds up.
No breathing. Respiratory arrest is marked by apnea.
Labored breathing or shortness of breath. Your slides call it painful. It is what the client feels.
Trouble breathing when lying flat on the back (supine).
Deep, fast, regular breathing that blows off CO₂. It happens in metabolic acidosis.
Breaths grow deeper and faster, then slower and shallower, then stop for a while. The cycle repeats.
Shallow breaths with irregular pauses (apnea), seen in central nervous system (CNS) disorders.
Collapse of alveoli, most often caused by a blocked airway.
Too much acid in the blood from a body-chemistry problem, such as diabetic ketoacidosis, not from the lungs.
Breathing in through the nose, then out slowly through pursed lips, to keep small airways open.

sections.heading: Three ways to describe a breathing problem
sections.keyIdea: Ask three questions: Can gas cross? Is the airway open? Is the pattern normal?
sections.body: Your slides sort oxygenation problems into three areas. Asking three questions helps you sort almost any breathing problem.
bullets: Gas exchange: Is oxygen crossing the alveoli into the blood, and is CO₂ getting out?
Airway patency: Is the airway open, or is something blocking or narrowing it?
Breathing pattern: Are the rate, depth, and rhythm normal?
sections.analogy: Picture a road (the airway) to a loading dock (the alveoli) where trucks (blood) pick up cargo (oxygen). Trouble can be a blocked road, a broken dock, or drivers who come too often, too rarely, or at random.

check.q: Thick mucus plugging the bronchi is which type of problem?
check.a: Airway patency. The airway is blocked.

sections.heading: Gas exchange problems: COPD
sections.keyIdea: In COPD, damaged alveoli can't trade gases well, so CO₂ builds up and oxygen stays low.
sections.body:
Damage to the chest structures (ribs, chest wall, pleura) can interfere with breathing. So can irritation or swelling of the airway lining.

A classic gas exchange problem is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In COPD, the alveoli are damaged. They can't exchange O₂ and CO₂ well. The result is CO₂ retention (CO₂ builds up, PaCO₂ above 45) and low blood oxygen.
bullets: Retractions: skin pulls in around the ribs because breathing takes so much work.
Cyanosis: bluish lips or nail beds from low oxygen.
Clubbed nail beds: a sign oxygen has been low for a long time.
sections.example: A client with long-standing COPD has clubbed fingers, uses neck muscles to breathe, and has a high CO₂. The body has adapted over years. That is why this client's oxygen target is often lower than other clients'. Clubbing is the old baseline. New retractions or cyanosis are what need action now.

sections.heading: Airway patency: mucus, swelling, collapse
sections.keyIdea: A blocked airway lets the air behind it be absorbed, and the alveoli collapse (atelectasis).
sections.body: Air must have an open path to reach the alveoli. Three things threaten that path. Mucus, foreign objects, and swelling can all close the tube.
bullets: Thick sputum can block large and small airways.
Inflammation from infection swells the airway lining and narrows it.
Airway obstruction is the main cause of atelectasis. Air trapped behind the block is absorbed, and alveoli collapse.
steps: Something reduces deep breathing or blocks an airway: pain after surgery, anesthesia, immobility, or mucus.
Air behind the block is absorbed. Alveoli collapse.
Blood passes collapsed alveoli without picking up oxygen. SpO₂ falls.
You hear diminished sounds or crackles at the bases. The client may breathe faster and have a low fever.
Treat the cause: control pain, then coach deep breathing, splinted coughing, incentive spirometry, turning, and walking.
sections.example: A client with three broken ribs on the left takes shallow breaths at 26/min and splints the chest. Pain 8/10, SpO₂ 92%, diminished sounds at the left base. Pain causes the shallow breathing, which causes atelectasis. Treat the pain as ordered so the client can breathe deeply. Never bind or wrap the chest. That limits breathing even more.

sections.heading: Rate words: too fast, too slow, none
sections.keyIdea: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ (alkalosis); hypoventilation keeps CO₂ in (acidosis).
sections.body:
Your slides use under 10 as the cutoff for bradypnea. Some textbooks use under 12. Use your course's number on exams.

Never assume fast breathing is just anxiety. Rule out low oxygen first.

table.caption: Rate and depth changes
rows: Fever, pain, anxiety, low oxygen, infection
Fast, deep breathing in and out
Too slow or shallow; too little O₂ reaches the lungs

sections.example: A 70-year-old with obstructive sleep apnea is 1 day after hip surgery and takes oral oxycodone. Opioids slow breathing, and sleep apnea already causes pauses. Check rate and sedation before every dose. Keep the head of the bed up, use continuous monitoring as ordered, and avoid other sedating drugs. If the rate falls below 10 with heavy sedation, rouse the client, support the airway, and call the provider.

check.q: A client in a panic attack breathes fast and deep and has tingling around the mouth. What is happening to the CO₂?
check.a: It is being blown off. Low CO₂ causes respiratory alkalosis, and tingling is a classic sign.

sections.heading: Dyspnea and orthopnea: what the client feels
sections.keyIdea: Dyspnea is what the client feels; orthopnea is breathlessness lying flat that improves when sitting up.
sections.body:
Dyspnea is labored breathing or shortness of breath. Your slides describe it as painful. Many sources describe it more broadly as uncomfortable breathing. Either way, it is subjective data. Ask the client to rate it, for example from 0 to 10. Ask what makes it better or worse.

Orthopnea is trouble breathing when lying flat. Lying down lets belly organs push up on the diaphragm. It also lets fluid spread across the lungs. Sitting up relieves it. If lying flat caused the distress, sit the client up first.

Document how many pillows the client needs to sleep. More pillows means things are getting worse.
sections.example: M.L. has trouble breathing when she lies down to sleep. She takes two puffs of her rescue inhaler and props herself up on 3 pillows. That is orthopnea, and it warns that she is getting worse. A few hours later she wakes up coughing, sweating, and dizzy, and she passes out.

sections.heading: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, and Biot
sections.keyIdea: Kussmaul fixes acid; Cheyne-Stokes waxes, wanes, and pauses; Biot is random and means brain trouble.
sections.body: These three named patterns show up often on exams. Each has a distinct look and a typical cause. Kussmaul is the body helping itself. Do not try to slow it. As the acidosis is corrected, Kussmaul breathing slows and CO₂ returns toward normal.

table.caption: Named breathing patterns
rows: Metabolic acidosis, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Blowing off CO₂ raises the pH.
Breaths grow deeper and faster, then slower and shallower, then apnea. Repeats.
Heart failure, increased intracranial pressure (ICP), drug overdose
Shallow breaths with irregular pauses; no pattern

bullets: A client with type 1 diabetes has glucose 520, fruity breath, and deep, regular breathing at 32/min. This is Kussmaul. The provider treats the cause.
A client with end-stage heart failure breathes deeper, then shallower, then stops for 20 seconds. Document Cheyne-Stokes.
A client with a brain injury now has clusters of shallow breaths with random 15–20 second pauses. The Glasgow Coma Scale score is falling. This is Biot. Call the provider now.
sections.analogy: Cheyne-Stokes is like a wave rolling in and out, then a calm pause. Biot is like static on a radio: random bursts and random silence.

check.q: Which named pattern is the body trying to fix a problem?
check.a: Kussmaul. It blows off CO₂ to make up for metabolic acidosis.

sections.heading: What can the nurse do without an order?
sections.keyIdea: Position, coach, pace, and clear secretions on your own; oxygen and medicine changes need an order.
sections.body:
Many helpful actions are independent. That means the nurse can do them without an order. They aim to improve gas exchange and breathing patterns. Medicines and changes to oxygen flow need a prescription.

For pursed-lip breathing, teach the client to breathe in through the nose for about 2 counts. Then breathe out slowly through pursed lips for about 4 counts. The slow, gentle exhale keeps small airways open so trapped air can get out. It is never forced.
bullets: Positioning: high Fowler's, or leaning forward over a table. The diaphragm drops, and the lungs expand.
Deep breathing exercises: slow, deep breaths open collapsed alveoli.
Pursed-lip breathing: in for 2, out slowly for 4.
Pace activities and help with ADLs: plan rest between tasks and watch activity tolerance.
Clear secretions: coughing, fluids as allowed, suctioning when needed.
Stay calm and coach: anxiety makes breathlessness worse.
sections.example: A client with COPD gets short of breath during morning care. SpO₂ is 90% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, and the target is 88–92%. The oxygen is already on target, so don't turn it up. Raise the head of the bed, pause the bath, coach pursed-lip breathing, and finish care in shorter steps.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Don't slow helpful breathing, don't bind broken ribs, and don't turn up oxygen that is already on target.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause the most errors. Use the right column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Both are fast and deep. Kussmaul comes with metabolic acidosis (high glucose, fruity breath). Panic gives tingling and alkalosis.
Cheyne-Stokes has a regular wave, then a pause. Biot is shallow and random.
Dyspnea is breathlessness in general. Orthopnea happens lying flat and eases sitting up.
Your slides say under 10. Some books say under 12. Use your course's number.
Don't raise the oxygen. Position, pace, and coach pursed-lip breathing.
Forcing air out hard collapses small airways. Out should be slow and gentle.
Clubbing is old. New retractions or cyanosis need action now.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Questions show a breathing pattern and ask you to name its cause or pick the right action.
sections.body: Common patterns you will see:
bullets: Name the pattern from a description (Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot)
Opioids plus sleep apnea: what to check before each dose
Rib fractures: treat pain, never bind the chest
Which action is independent vs. needs an order
Evaluating pursed-lip breathing teaching
steps: Read the stem: "A client with diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deeply and rapidly with a regular rhythm. What should the nurse do?"
What is it really asking? Is this breathing a problem to stop, or a helpful response?
Key cues: metabolic acidosis, deep and regular, fast rate.
Wrong: "coach slower breathing" fights the body's fix. "Give a sedative" weakens the compensation. "Reassure the client it is anxiety" misses the acidosis.
Answer: keep monitoring and support the provider's treatment of the acidosis. Kussmaul is compensation.
Strategy: first ask, "Is this breathing helping the client or harming them?" Treat the cause, not the helpful response.

sections.heading: Worked case: opioid and a quiet night
sections.keyIdea: Slow, shallow breathing with heavy sedation after an opioid needs you to rouse the client and support the airway first.
sections.body: One hour after IV morphine, a 72-year-old with sleep apnea breathes 8 times a minute. The client is hard to wake. SpO₂ is 89%. The head of the bed is flat.
steps: Notice: RR 8, hard to wake, low SpO₂, flat in bed, recent opioid, sleep apnea.
Name it: bradypnea and hypoventilation. CO₂ is building up (respiratory acidosis).
Act first: rouse the client and support the airway. Raise the head of the bed.
Then: give oxygen as ordered and notify the provider. Hold further opioid doses until reassessed.
Evaluate: rate above 10, easier to wake, SpO₂ improving.

check.q: Why are this client's risks multiplied?
check.a: Sleep apnea, older age, and opioids all slow or pause breathing. Together they raise the risk of dangerous hypoventilation.

pearls: Kussmaul = deep, fast, regular = metabolic acidosis. Treat the cause, not the breathing.
Cheyne-Stokes = crescendo, decrescendo, pause. Biot = shallow and chaotic with apnea.
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ (tingling, lightheaded). Hypoventilation raises CO₂ (drowsy, headache).
Rib fractures: treat the pain so the client can breathe deeply. Never bind the chest.
Sleep apnea plus opioids: check rate and sedation before every dose and keep the head up.
Pursed-lip breathing: in through the nose, out slowly through pursed lips, about twice as long out. Never forced.
redFlags: New Biot or Cheyne-Stokes breathing with a falling level of consciousness after brain injury: call the provider now.
Rate under 10 in a sedated client after an opioid: rouse, support the airway, call the provider.
Apnea: respiratory arrest. Call for help and start rescue breathing or CPR per protocol.
New orthopnea or needing more pillows to sleep: the condition is worsening. Assess and report.

checks.q: A client breathes deeply and rapidly with a regular rhythm, and labs show metabolic acidosis. Should you coach slower breathing?
checks.a: No. This is Kussmaul breathing, which blows off CO₂ to raise the pH. The provider treats the acidosis.

checks.q: Why is atelectasis common after abdominal surgery?
checks.a: Pain and anesthesia cause shallow breathing and less coughing. Airways plug, and alveoli collapse.

checks.q: A client with emphysema says, "I push the air out as hard and fast as I can." Did pursed-lip teaching work?
checks.a: No. Breathing out should be slow and gentle, about twice as long as breathing in. Forcing it collapses small airways.

checks.q: Which pattern cycles from deep to shallow breaths, then apnea, in heart failure?
checks.a: Cheyne-Stokes respirations.

checks.q: A COPD client is short of breath, SpO₂ 90% on target. Which actions are independent?
checks.a: Raising the head of the bed, pacing care, and coaching pursed-lip breathing. Changing oxygen flow needs an order.

topics.title: Diagnostic Tests: ABGs, Pulse Oximetry, and More
topics.summary: ABGs show oxygen and acid–base balance, pulse oximetry shows a quick trend, and other tests show what is happening inside the lungs.
objectives: You can state normal values for pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, PaO₂, and SaO₂.
You can read an ABG step by step and name the imbalance and its compensation.
You can explain what pulse oximetry measures and when it can mislead you.
You can describe nursing care before and after a sputum test, PFTs, and peak flow.
You can describe nursing care for chest x-ray, angiogram, V/Q scan, bronchoscopy, and thoracentesis.
topics.bigPicture:
Your assessment tells you a client looks short of oxygen. Tests tell you how much, why, and where. The most important one is the arterial blood gas (ABG). It shows oxygen levels and acid–base balance in one sample.

In the M.L. case, her SpO₂ rose from 85% to 90–93% on a face mask. But her ABG showed severe respiratory acidosis. Her lungs could no longer blow off CO₂. She was tiring out. Reading an ABG is just a short routine you repeat every time.
recap: Normals: pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO₂ 35–45; HCO₃⁻ 22–26; PaO₂ 80–100; SaO₂ 95–100%.
CO₂ is the lungs' acid. HCO₃⁻ is the kidneys' base. Over 45 CO₂ is hypercarbia; under 35 is hypocarbia.
Read in order: pH → CO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → match → compensation → oxygen.
ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.
SpO₂ shows oxygen saturation only. It says nothing about CO₂ and can mislead with anemia or carbon monoxide.
After an ABG: firm pressure at least 5 minutes (10 or more on anticoagulants), then check the hand.
Bronchoscopy: NPO until the gag reflex returns. Thoracentesis: sit up, lean forward, stay still, then watch for pneumothorax.
In an asthma attack, a normal or rising CO₂ means the client is tiring. Escalate.

keyTerms.def: A blood sample from an artery that measures pH, CO₂, bicarbonate, and oxygen.
How acidic or basic the blood is. Normal is 7.35–7.45.
The amount of carbon dioxide in arterial blood. Normal 35–45 mm Hg. The lungs control it, and it acts as an acid.
A base controlled mainly by the kidneys. Normal about 22–26 mEq/L.
The amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood (plasma). Normal about 80–100 mm Hg.
The percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, measured in an arterial sample. Normal about 95–100%.
Oxygen saturation estimated by a pulse oximeter. The "p" stands for pulse.
CO₂ above 45 mm Hg: too much CO₂.
CO₂ below 35 mm Hg: too little CO₂.
The other system (lungs or kidneys) adjusting to push the pH back toward normal.
A blood thinner. It makes bleeding after a puncture last longer.
How fast a person can blow air out, measured with a small hand-held meter.
A flexible scope passed into the airways to look inside, remove secretions, or take a biopsy.
A needle placed through the chest wall to remove fluid from the pleural space.

sections.heading: What does an ABG measure?
sections.keyIdea: An ABG shows two things at once: how well the client is oxygenating and whether the blood is too acidic or too basic.
sections.body:
An ABG is drawn from an artery, usually the radial artery at the wrist. Arterial blood shows what the lungs have just done.

Oxygen. SaO₂ is the percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. PaO₂ is the amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood. SaO₂ is a percent; PaO₂ is an amount. If both are low, the client has hypoxemia.

Acid–base. pH tells you if the blood is acidic or basic. CO₂ is the lungs' part, and it acts like an acid. More CO₂ means more acid. HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) is the kidneys' part, and it is a base.
sections.analogy: Think of pH as a seesaw. CO₂ sits on the acid side; bicarbonate sits on the base side. The lungs change CO₂ in minutes. The kidneys change bicarbonate slowly, over hours to days.

sections.heading: How do you read an ABG?
sections.keyIdea: Use the same six steps every time, in the same order.
sections.body: Don't try to do it all at once. Go one value at a time. Write an arrow next to each one if that helps.
steps: pH: under 7.35 = acidosis. Over 7.45 = alkalosis. 7.35–7.45 = normal or fully compensated.
PaCO₂: acid (over 45), base (under 35), or normal?
HCO₃⁻: acid (under 22), base (over 26), or normal?
Match: the value that matches the pH direction is the cause. CO₂ matches = respiratory. HCO₃⁻ matches = metabolic.

Compensation: other value normal = uncompensated. Other value abnormal and pointing the opposite way (base vs. acid), with pH still abnormal = partly compensated. pH normal with both abnormal = fully compensated.
Oxygen: low PaO₂ and SaO₂ = hypoxemia.
sections.example: An hour after IV morphine, a client is hard to wake, RR 8. ABG: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 58, HCO₃⁻ 24, PaO₂ 68. The pH is low (acidosis). CO₂ is high (acid), so it matches. HCO₃⁻ is normal. This is uncompensated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia. Slow breathing let CO₂ build up. Rouse the client, support the airway, and call the provider.

check.q: A crying client breathes 34/min with tingling around the mouth. pH 7.51, PaCO₂ 28, HCO₃⁻ 24. What is it?
check.a: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis. Fast breathing blew off CO₂, and bicarbonate is still normal. Treat the cause of the fast breathing.

sections.heading: What is compensation?
sections.keyIdea: When one system causes the problem, the other system shifts the opposite way to pull the pH back toward normal.
sections.body:
The lungs and kidneys help each other. If the problem is respiratory, the kidneys slowly adjust bicarbonate. If the problem is metabolic, the lungs quickly change breathing. That is why you see Kussmaul breathing in metabolic acidosis.

ROME helps you spot the cause. In a respiratory problem, pH and PaCO₂ move in opposite directions. In a metabolic problem, pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the same (equal) direction.

If the pH is normal but both values are abnormal, look at which side of 7.40 the pH sits on. That side names the original problem.

table.caption: The four main imbalances
rows: Hypoventilation: opioids, tiring asthma client, COPD

sections.example: A client with a 40-pack-year COPD history has usual shortness of breath on exertion. ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 56, HCO₃⁻ 31, PaO₂ 62. The pH is normal, but both values are high. pH is on the acid side of 7.40, and CO₂ is the acid. This is fully compensated respiratory acidosis, the client's baseline. The kidneys kept bicarbonate for years.

sections.heading: What is the nurse's job for an ABG?
sections.keyIdea: Arterial blood is under high pressure, so hold firm pressure and then check the hand's circulation.
sections.body: An ABG comes from an artery. Blood there is under high pressure, so bleeding is the main risk afterward. The oxygen result also only makes sense if you know what the client was breathing.
bullets: Note on the requisition whether the client is on room air or oxygen, and at what flow.
After the puncture, hold firm, direct pressure for at least 5 minutes.
Hold 10 minutes or more if the client takes an anticoagulant.
Check the site for bleeding or swelling.
Check the hand: color, warmth, capillary refill, and pulse. Report pallor, coolness, numbness, or slow refill promptly.

check.q: A client on an anticoagulant just had a radial ABG. How long do you hold pressure?
check.a: Firm pressure for 10 minutes or longer. Then check the site and the circulation to the hand.

sections.heading: When can pulse oximetry fool you?
sections.keyIdea: SpO₂ is a trend tool: it ignores CO₂ and can read wrong, so always match it to the client.
sections.body:
A pulse oximeter clips on a finger, toe, or earlobe. It shines light through the tissue to estimate SpO₂. It is painless and continuous, which is great for trends. A common normal range is 95–100%. Some clients who retain CO₂, such as some with COPD, have a lower target, often 88–92%.

SpO₂ measures oxygenation. PaCO₂ measures ventilation. A client can have a normal SpO₂ while CO₂ is dangerously high. When the number doesn't match the client, fix the measurement and assess the client before changing therapy.
bullets: Poor circulation (cold hands, low blood pressure): weak or wrong signal.
Movement or shivering: unreliable reading.
Dark nail polish or artificial nails: can block the light.
Darker skin: devices may read falsely high. Look at the client, not just the number.
Severe anemia: SpO₂ can look normal while total oxygen is low.
Carbon monoxide (smoke, faulty heaters): SpO₂ may read normal or high while the client is severely hypoxic. An ABG with a carboxyhemoglobin level is needed.
sections.example: The monitor reads 97%, but the client is confused, breathing 30/min, with bluish lips. Believe the client. Check the probe and waveform, try another site, and call the provider. An ABG may be needed.

sections.heading: Tests that need the client's effort
sections.keyIdea: Sputum, PFTs, incentive spirometry, and peak flow all depend on good teaching and good timing.
sections.body: These tests need the client to work with you. Good teaching gives good results. For sputum, collect before the first antibiotic. But never delay a due antibiotic waiting for a morning specimen.
bullets: Sputum specimen: finds the organism causing infection (culture and sensitivity). Early morning is best, since secretions pool overnight. Rinse with water only, no mouthwash. Take deep breaths, then cough from deep in the chest into a sterile cup. Saliva is not acceptable.
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): the client breathes into a machine that measures lung volumes and airflow. They help find asthma and COPD. No smoking before, and hold inhalers only as instructed.
Incentive spirometry: a hand-held device that coaches slow, deep breaths to open the lungs and clear mucus. Common after surgery.
Peak flow (PEFR): measures how fast the client can blow air out. People with asthma use it at home and compare to their personal best.

table.caption: Peak flow zones (asthma action plan)
rows: Good control. Keep the usual plan.
Caution. Use rescue medicine and follow the plan.
Medical alert. Use rescue medicine and get emergency care.

sections.heading: Imaging and procedures inside the chest
sections.keyIdea: Know what each test shows and the one or two safety points the nurse owns.
sections.body: These tests look inside the chest. For each one, know what it shows and the nurse's key safety steps. Watch for pneumothorax after any procedure that enters the chest.

table.caption: Imaging and invasive tests
rows: Pneumonia, collapse, fluid, air in the pleural space
Remove metal from the chest area. Ask about pregnancy and report it before the x-ray. M.L.'s x-ray showed pneumonia.
Blood flow in lung arteries using IV contrast dye, such as a clot
Before: check kidney function and past contrast reactions; report problems. After: check the catheter site.
Compares airflow and blood flow in each area, looking for mismatch like a clot
Explain two parts: an inhaled tracer and an IV tracer.
Direct look inside the airways; can remove mucus or take a biopsy
NPO before. After: NPO until the gag reflex returns. Sore throat, drowsiness, and blood-streaked sputum are expected. Stridor, chest pain, fast breathing, or falling SpO₂ are not.
Removes fluid from the pleural space
Sit upright, leaning forward over a table. Stay still and don't cough during the needle. After: watch for pneumothorax and bleeding.

sections.example: One hour after a thoracentesis removed 900 mL of fluid, the client has sudden sharp chest pain and shortness of breath. Breath sounds are absent on the right. SpO₂ dropped from 95% to 88%. Suspect a pneumothorax. Stay with the client, raise the head of the bed, give oxygen per protocol, and call the provider now.

check.q: Why stay NPO after bronchoscopy until the gag reflex returns?
check.a: The throat was numbed. Without a gag reflex, the client could aspirate food or fluid into the lungs.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most ABG and test errors come from mixing up percent vs. amount, partial vs. full compensation, or trusting SpO₂ alone.
sections.body: These look-alikes cost the most points. Use the right column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: SaO₂ is a percent on hemoglobin. PaO₂ is an amount dissolved in blood.
pH still abnormal = partly. pH back to normal = fully.
Respiratory: pH and CO₂ go opposite ways. Metabolic: pH and HCO₃⁻ go the same way.
SpO₂ ignores CO₂, anemia, and carbon monoxide.
Normal CO₂ in an asthma attack
Not reassuring. The client is tiring and can't blow CO₂ off.
Collect sputum first if you can, but don't delay a due antibiotic.
Sore throat and streaks of blood are expected. Stridor is an emergency.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect ABG interpretation, test preparation, and post-procedure complications.
sections.body: Common patterns you will see:
bullets: Interpret an ABG and name the compensation
Choose the client whose ABG needs action first (acute beats chronic)
When SpO₂ doesn't match the client
Order of sputum culture and first antibiotic
Positioning and complications for thoracentesis and bronchoscopy
steps: Read the stem: "pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 52, HCO₃⁻ 30. How should the nurse interpret this?"
What is it really asking? Name the imbalance and whether it is compensated.
Key cues: pH low (acidosis). CO₂ high (acid) matches. HCO₃⁻ high (base) is moving the other way.
Wrong: "metabolic acidosis" needs a low HCO₃⁻. "Fully compensated" needs a normal pH. "Uncompensated" needs a normal HCO₃⁻.
Answer: partly compensated respiratory acidosis.
Strategy: always go pH, then CO₂, then HCO₃⁻. Decide the cause before you think about compensation.

sections.heading: Worked case: M.L. is tiring out
sections.keyIdea: Rising CO₂ in a breathless asthma client means exhaustion, not improvement.
sections.body: M.L. arrives in the emergency department with SpO₂ 85%. On a face mask, it rises to 90–93%. But her breath sounds are decreased, and her SpO₂ starts to fall again. Her ABG shows severe respiratory acidosis.
steps: Notice: SpO₂ only partly better and falling again, decreased breath sounds.
Read the ABG: pH low, CO₂ high and matching. This is respiratory acidosis.
Interpret: early in an attack, fast breathing lowers CO₂. A high CO₂ means she can no longer blow it off.
Act: stay with her, call for help, and prepare for ventilatory support.
Remember: the SpO₂ looked better, but the ABG showed the real danger.

check.q: Why was the improved SpO₂ misleading for M.L.?
check.a: SpO₂ shows only oxygen saturation. It says nothing about CO₂, which was rising because she was too tired to breathe it off.

mnemonics.name: ROME
mnemonics.text: Respiratory Opposite: pH and PaCO₂ move in opposite directions. Metabolic Equal: pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the same direction.

pearls: SaO₂ is a percent; PaO₂ is an amount. Both low = hypoxemia.
Normal pH with two abnormal values = fully compensated. The side of 7.40 names the original problem.
In an asthma attack, a normal or rising CO₂ is a bad sign. The client is tiring.
SpO₂ says nothing about CO₂. A well-saturated client can still be retaining CO₂.
Sputum culture: water rinse, deep cough, before antibiotics, but never delay a due antibiotic.
Before contrast studies, check kidney function and past contrast reactions.
redFlags: SpO₂ that doesn't match the client (97% but confused and blue): trust the client, reassess, call the provider.
Sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, absent breath sounds, or falling SpO₂ after thoracentesis or bronchoscopy: suspect pneumothorax; call now.
Stridor after bronchoscopy: airway swelling. Call for help.
Peak flow under 50% of personal best, especially after rescue medicine: emergency care now.
Worsening respiratory acidosis despite oxygen: the client is tiring. Expect ventilatory support.

checks.q: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 40, HCO₃⁻ 17. What is it?
checks.a: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis. pH and bicarbonate are both low (same direction), and CO₂ is normal.

checks.q: A client with dark nail polish and cold hands has SpO₂ 84% but is talking comfortably with pink lips. What do you do?
checks.a: Suspect a false reading. Warm the hand or move the probe to an earlobe, remove polish, and assess the client before acting.

checks.q: How should a client sit for a thoracentesis, and why?
checks.a: Upright, leaning forward over a table. This spreads the ribs and lets fluid collect at the base where the needle goes in.

checks.q: A sputum culture is ordered, and the first antibiotic dose is due now. Which comes first?
checks.a: Collect the sputum first so the antibiotic doesn't affect the culture. Then give the antibiotic promptly. Don't wait for a morning specimen.

checks.q: A client was rescued from a house fire. SpO₂ is 99%. Can you relax?
checks.a: No. Pulse oximeters can't tell carbon monoxide from oxygen. Give high-flow oxygen as ordered, often by nonrebreather, and expect an ABG with a carboxyhemoglobin level.

topics.title: Oxygen Therapy and Delivery Devices
topics.summary: Oxygen is a medication. It needs an order, the right device and flow, a target saturation, fire safety, and a nurse who checks that it works.
objectives: You can explain when oxygen is needed and why the airway must be open first.
You can compare the nasal cannula, simple mask, nonrebreather, and Venturi mask.
You can apply oxygen in the correct order and check the whole system on rounds.
You can titrate oxygen for a client who retains CO₂ and spot CO₂ narcosis.
You can teach home oxygen fire safety.
You can tell when oxygen is not working and escalate.
topics.bigPicture:
Oxygen is so common that it is easy to forget it is a drug. It has a dose (flow and concentration), a route (the device), a reason (low saturation or signs of hypoxia), and side effects. It needs a medical order.

Follow M.L.: 91% on room air, then 4 L/min by nasal cannula. In the ER she was at 85%. She went on 8 L/min by face mask, then 10 L/min, and still kept falling. She needed a breathing tube and a ventilator. Nurses match the device to the need and notice when a device is not enough.
recap: Oxygen is a medication: it needs an order with a device, a flow, and usually a target SpO₂.
No device works unless the airway is open. Open the airway first.
Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min. Simple mask 5–10 (at least 5). Nonrebreather 10–15. Venturi = precise FiO₂.
Apply in order: verify, set and confirm flow, apply, reassess.
Nonrebreather bag must never collapse when the client breathes in. Turn up the flow.
CO₂ retainers: titrate to 88–92%. New drowsiness after more oxygen = check CO₂. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client.
Fire safety: no smoking, flames, or petroleum products; cylinders upright and secured.
Still hypoxic on 6 L by cannula, or worse on a nonrebreather: escalate.

keyTerms.def: Fraction of inspired oxygen: the percent of oxygen in the air the client breathes in. Room air is about 21%.
How many liters of oxygen per minute (L/min) come from the flowmeter.
The wall device that sets the oxygen flow. Read it at the middle of the ball.
An open, unblocked airway.
Soft tubing with two short prongs in the nostrils. The most common low-flow device.
A mask over nose and mouth that gives a moderate oxygen level. Needs at least 5 L/min.
A mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves. It gives the highest oxygen of the standard masks.
A mask with color-coded adapters that gives a precise, set oxygen percent.
Adjust a dose up or down to reach a target, such as keeping SpO₂ in a set range.
Buildup of carbon dioxide in the blood, common in some clients with COPD.
Drowsiness and confusion caused by a high CO₂ level.

sections.heading: When does a client need oxygen?
sections.keyIdea: Low saturation plus signs of hypoxia means oxygen, but only after the airway is open.
sections.body:
The need for oxygen is shown by a low oxygen saturation. At the bedside, that means a low SpO₂ or PaO₂ with signs of hypoxia. Look for restlessness, confusion, fast heart rate, fast breathing, hard work to breathe, or cyanosis.

The order includes a device, a flow rate or percent, and often a target SpO₂. In an emergency, facility protocols let nurses start oxygen first and get the order right after.

Noninvasive devices need a patent airway to work. A cannula or mask only delivers oxygen to the top of the airway. If the tongue, mucus, or swelling blocks it, oxygen never reaches the alveoli.
sections.example: A drowsy client in recovery has loud snoring breaths, retractions above the sternum, and little chest rise. SpO₂ fell from 96% to 89% on 2 L/min. Turning up the oxygen won't help. The tongue is blocking the airway. Reposition the head and jaw first, then reassess.
sections.analogy: Oxygen on a blocked airway is like turning up the water on a kinked hose. More flow does nothing until you straighten the hose.

sections.heading: Meet the devices
sections.keyIdea: Devices differ in how much oxygen they give and how exact that amount is; Venturi is the most exact.
sections.body: These are the devices you will use most as a new nurse. They differ in how much oxygen they give and how precise the dose is. As a rough rule, a nasal cannula adds about 4% oxygen for each liter above room air (21%).

table.caption: Common oxygen devices
rows: Client can eat and talk. Still works with mouth breathing. Humidify higher flows per policy. Check skin behind ears and at the nostrils.
Needs 5 L/min or more to flush exhaled CO₂ out of the mask. Must come off to eat.
Highest of the standard masks. One-way valves keep exhaled air out of the bag. Bag must stay inflated. For severe, sudden hypoxemia.
Most precise. Color-coded adapters mix a fixed amount of room air. Good for COPD with CO₂ retention. Keep side ports open.

check.q: The provider wants a COPD client to get exactly 28% oxygen. Which device?
check.a: A Venturi mask. It gives a precise, set percent if the adapter is right and the side ports stay open.

sections.heading: How do you apply oxygen safely?
sections.keyIdea: Verify, set and confirm flow, apply, then reassess, just like any medication.
sections.body:
Oxygen is a medication, so use the same safety checks as any drug. Set the flow before the device touches the client. That way oxygen reaches them right away.

For a nonrebreather, fill the reservoir bag before putting the mask on. The AP may measure and report SpO₂. The RN assesses, titrates, teaches, and evaluates.
steps: Verify the order (device, flow, target). Do hand hygiene. Use two client identifiers.
Explain the procedure. Connect the tubing (and humidifier if used) to the flowmeter.
Set the prescribed flow. Read the flowmeter at the middle of the ball.
Confirm oxygen is flowing from the prongs. You can feel or hear it.
Place the curved prongs in the nostrils, curving down. Loop tubing over the ears and snug the slider under the chin.
Reassess SpO₂, breathing rate and effort, mental status, and the skin at the ears and nose.
sections.example: The order says oxygen at 3 L/min by simple face mask. A simple mask needs at least 5 L/min, or the client rebreathes CO₂. Call the provider to clarify. A cannula at 3 L/min or a mask at 5–10 L/min would both work. Don't switch devices without an order.

check.q: Why set and confirm the flow before placing the prongs?
check.a: So the client gets oxygen as soon as the device is on, and never breathes through empty tubing.

sections.heading: What do you check on every round?
sections.keyIdea: When SpO₂ falls on oxygen, trace the whole system from the wall to the client before anything else.
sections.body: Once oxygen is on, keep it working and keep the client safe. If SpO₂ drops, look for a delivery problem first. A kinked tube is faster to fix than a new order.
bullets: Flowmeter: at the prescribed rate.
Tubing: connected, not kinked, not pinched under side rails or the client.
Fit: prongs in the nose; mask snug but not tight.
Skin: behind the ears, over the nose, at the nostrils. Pad as needed. Tubing can cause pressure injuries.
Humidifier: filled if used.
Client: SpO₂, breathing rate and effort, heart rate, mental status, color.
Nonrebreather: if the bag collapses when the client breathes in, increase the flow (up to 15 L/min). Check that valves are intact.
sections.example: On rounds, a client on 4 L/min by cannula has tubing pinched under the side rail. SpO₂ is 91%, down from 95%. The skin behind both ears is red. A visitor is putting petroleum balm on the client's lips. The client breathes through the mouth while watching TV. Fix the tubing, the falling SpO₂, the skin, and the balm. Mouth breathing is fine. Oxygen still pools in the nose and throat.

sections.heading: Clients who retain CO₂: is more better?
sections.keyIdea: Titrate to 88–92% for CO₂ retainers, but never withhold oxygen from a client who is hypoxemic.
sections.body:
Some clients, especially with COPD, live with high CO₂ levels. Giving them high oxygen without a target can push CO₂ even higher. The result is CO₂ narcosis. The client becomes drowsy and confused and may stop breathing well.

So providers often order oxygen titrated to a target of 88–92%. A Venturi mask helps when a precise, low dose is needed. A titration order works both ways. Turn the oxygen down when SpO₂ is above the target.

Here is the critical balance. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client in distress. Low oxygen kills faster than high CO₂. Give it, titrate to target, and watch mental status, rate, SpO₂, and ABGs.
sections.example: A COPD client has an order to keep SpO₂ 88–92%. A family member turned the flow to 6 L/min. The client was alert an hour ago. Now the client is hard to wake, SpO₂ 98%, RR 12. Lower the oxygen to reach the target, but don't turn it off. Notify the provider and expect an ABG to check CO₂. Teach the family that more is not always better.

check.q: A COPD client's SpO₂ is 84%, and the client is struggling to breathe. Do you hold oxygen because they retain CO₂?
check.a: No. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client. Apply it, titrate to the target, and watch mental status and CO₂.

sections.heading: How do you keep oxygen fire-safe?
sections.keyIdea: Oxygen doesn't burn by itself, but it makes any spark burn hotter and faster.
sections.body: Oxygen is not flammable by itself. But it helps fires start more easily and burn hotter and faster. That is why the safety rules are strict. Any heat or spark source near oxygen needs correction right away. Teach clients and families these rules.
bullets: No smoking by anyone in the room or home. Post "No Smoking: Oxygen in Use" signs.
Keep oxygen away from open flames and heat: candles, gas stoves, fireplaces, space heaters.
Use water-based lubricant for dry lips and nose. Never petroleum jelly or oil-based products.
Store cylinders upright and secured in a stand or cart so they can't fall.
