Use only the prescribed flow. If breathing gets worse, call the provider instead of turning it up.
Check tank levels before leaving home or during transport. Keep tubing from being crushed.
sections.analogy: Oxygen is like a bellows on a campfire. It doesn't light the fire, but it turns a tiny spark into a big blaze fast.

sections.heading: Is the oxygen working?
sections.keyIdea: Oxygen is working when the body's alarm signs calm down; if they don't, escalate.
sections.body:
After every change, reassess. Oxygen is working when SpO₂ reaches target, breathing slows and eases, heart rate falls, alertness improves, and color gets better.

It is not working when SpO₂ stays low, breathing stays fast with neck muscles working, or new restlessness or confusion appears. A cannula tops out at about 6 L/min. Still low at that level means the device has maxed out. Tell the provider so a bigger device can be ordered.

A client who keeps getting worse on high-flow masks may need a breathing tube and ventilator. Watch for rising CO₂, falling alertness, and exhaustion.
sections.example: One hour after a pneumonia client went up to 6 L/min by cannula, SpO₂ is 87%. RR 32 with neck muscles working, plus new restlessness and confusion. The oxygen is not working. Raise the head of the bed, stay, and call the provider or rapid response. Compare a client who now speaks full sentences, whose HR fell from 118 to 96, with pink lips. That client is improving.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: The traps are wrong flow for the device, skipping the airway, and treating the number instead of the client.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause the most errors. Use the right column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Simple mask needs at least 5 L/min. Cannula runs 1–6. An order outside the range must be clarified.
Venturi = precise, often low percent. Nonrebreather = highest percent for severe hypoxemia.
Snoring and retractions mean blocked airway. Reposition before turning up the flow.
New drowsiness after an oxygen increase in a CO₂ retainer is narcosis until proven otherwise.
A normal SpO₂ on oxygen doesn't prove ventilation is enough. Check rate and alertness.
Not a problem. The SpO₂ tells you if it works.
Petroleum near oxygen can burn. Use water-based only.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect questions on matching device to need, troubleshooting, CO₂ retainers, and fire safety.
sections.body: Common patterns you will see:
bullets: Which device gives a precise 28%?
An order that doesn't fit the device (simple mask at 3 L/min)
A COPD client getting drowsy after an oxygen increase
Home oxygen teaching that needs correction
Signs oxygen is or isn't working; when to escalate
steps: Read the stem: "A client on a nonrebreather at 10 L/min has a reservoir bag that collapses with each breath. What is the priority?"
What is it really asking? What does a collapsing bag mean, and what fixes it?
Key cues: nonrebreather, bag collapses when breathing in.
Wrong: "switch to a cannula" lowers the oxygen. "Remove the mask" stops oxygen. "Call the provider first" delays a fix you can make now.
Answer: increase the flow until the bag stays inflated, then reassess.
Strategy: if you have an order or protocol that fixes the problem, use it first. Escalate if the client doesn't respond.

sections.heading: Worked case: when the device isn't enough
sections.keyIdea: Each step up in oxygen is a test; if the client keeps falling, the next step is escalation, not waiting.
sections.body: M.L. is on 4 L/min by nasal cannula in the clinic. In the ER her SpO₂ is 85%. She goes on 8 L/min by face mask, then 10 L/min. Her SpO₂ keeps falling, and her breath sounds are decreased. She is tiring out.
steps: Notice: SpO₂ falling despite more oxygen, decreased breath sounds, signs she is tiring.
Interpret: the devices are not enough, and she is tiring. This is respiratory failure.
Act: stay with her, raise the head of the bed, and call the provider or rapid response.
Anticipate: a breathing tube and mechanical ventilation, as M.L. needed.
Evaluate: after each change, recheck SpO₂, effort, and mental status.

check.q: If M.L.'s breathing rate also slowed and she became drowsy, would that be a good sign?
check.a: No. She would be too tired to keep breathing fast, not calming down. Slowing breathing with drowsiness and falling SpO₂ means respiratory failure. Escalate now.

pearls: Oxygen is a medication: order, device, flow, and usually a target SpO₂.
Simple face mask: at least 5 L/min. Clarify any order below that.
Nonrebreather: prefill the bag, and never let it collapse when the client breathes in.
Precise percent (such as 28%) = Venturi mask.
COPD with CO₂ retention: aim for 88–92%. New drowsiness after more oxygen = check CO₂.
No petroleum products near oxygen. Use water-based lubricant.
redFlags: SpO₂ falling despite more oxygen (like M.L. on 10 L/min by mask): call the provider or rapid response; expect intubation.
COPD client on oxygen who becomes drowsy or confused: lower oxygen to target, call the provider, expect an ABG.
Snoring breaths, retractions, and falling SpO₂ in a sedated client: open the airway first.
Smoking, open flames, or petroleum products near oxygen: stop and correct now.

checks.q: A client going home on oxygen says, "I'll put Vaseline in my nose so it doesn't crack." Your response?
checks.a: Correct it. Petroleum products can burn near oxygen. Use a water-based lubricant instead.

checks.q: Why does a nasal cannula still work when the client breathes through the mouth?
checks.a: Oxygen fills the nose and back of the throat and is drawn in with each breath, even through the mouth.

checks.q: A client on 2 L/min by cannula is restless with SpO₂ 86%. The airway is clear. What do you do?
checks.a: Raise the head of the bed, increase oxygen per order or protocol, stay with the client, and call the provider. Reassess SpO₂, effort, and mental status.

checks.q: Which findings show oxygen is working?
checks.a: SpO₂ at target, slower and easier breathing, a falling heart rate, better alertness, and pink oral mucosa.

checks.q: A COPD client with a target of 88–92% has SpO₂ 97%. What does the titration order tell you to do?
checks.a: Turn the oxygen down to reach the target. Titration works in both directions.

topics.title: Oxygenation Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: A baby's tiny airway, a pregnant client's raised diaphragm, and an older adult's weak cough change how oxygen problems look and how fast they turn dangerous.
objectives: You can explain why infants, young children, and older adults are at higher risk.
You can tell normal pediatric breathing from signs of respiratory distress.
You can respond to a choking infant and recognize a toddler's inhaled object.
You can list normal breathing changes of pregnancy and findings that need follow-up.
You can spot quiet signs of pneumonia in older adults and teach aspiration prevention.
You can interpret hemoglobin and hematocrit by sex and name genetic influences.
topics.bigPicture:
A breathing rate of 44 is normal for a 6-month-old. In a 40-year-old, it is serious trouble. Belly breathing is normal in a toddler. Mild breathlessness on stairs is normal late in pregnancy. Crackles at the bases can be common at 85. To assess well, you must know what is normal for this person.

Children under 1 year and older adults are at higher risk for oxygen problems. Young children get sick from lung illness more easily. Older adults have more health problems that affect breathing. First rule out what is normal for the client. The new change left over is the priority.
recap: Children under 1 and older adults are at the highest risk for oxygen problems.
Children: short, narrow airways; immature lungs; belly breathing under age 6; high risk of choking.
Retractions, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing, and stridor at rest mean distress, even if the rate looks normal for age.
Choking infant: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 chest thrusts, head down. No abdominal thrusts.
Pregnancy lowers CO₂, not O₂. Slightly alkaline pH is expected; SpO₂ under 95% is not.
Pregnant client: avoid lying flat on the back. If she becomes hypotensive supine, turn her to her side.
Older adults may have pneumonia without fever: new confusion, weakness, poor appetite, fast HR and RR.
Aspiration precautions: upright to eat and after meals, small bites, no talking while chewing.

keyTerms.def: Skin pulling inward between the ribs, below the ribs, or above the sternum when breathing in. A sign of distress.
How hard it is to move air through the airway. Narrow airways have more resistance.
Bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk in a newborn. Normal.
A sunken, caved-in sternum.
A sternum that sticks out ("pigeon chest").
A round chest where front-to-back width equals side-to-side width. Normal in infants; not normal after about age 6.
A crackling feel under the skin. In a newborn near the collarbone, it can mean a broken clavicle.
Air left in the lungs after breathing out. It acts as an oxygen reserve.
Stuffy nose caused by pregnancy changes in the nasal lining.
Forward curve of the upper spine (hunched back). It can limit lung expansion.
Breathing food, fluid, stomach contents, or an object into the airway and lungs.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease: stomach contents flow back up into the esophagus, raising aspiration risk.
The percent of blood made up of red blood cells.

sections.heading: Why are young children at higher risk?
sections.keyIdea: A child's airway is small and narrow, so a little swelling or mucus blocks a lot of airflow.
sections.body: Children are not just small adults. Their bodies are built differently, and they have less reserve. They can go from okay to very sick fast. Your slides list these differences.
bullets: Shorter, narrower airway. A little swelling or mucus raises airway resistance a lot.
The trachea splits higher and at a different angle than in adults.
Lung tissue is not fully developed at birth. Diseases of the alveoli can hit harder.
Children under 6 breathe mainly with the diaphragm. The belly rises more than the chest. That is normal.
Higher risk of airway blockage from objects and infection. Young children put things in their mouths.
Upper respiratory infections are common in children but usually not serious.
sections.analogy: Picture a drinking straw and a garden hose. Coat each inside with the same thin layer of mud. The hose still carries water, but the straw is nearly blocked. A child's airway is the straw.

sections.heading: Normal child or child in distress?
sections.keyIdea: Judge a child's rate by age, but act on effort signs like retractions, grunting, and stridor at rest.
sections.body:
Always compare a child's rate to the range for that age. Distress signs matter more than a rate that only looks fast. A child in distress needs to be kept upright and calm and given oxygen as ordered. Don't lay the child flat or upset them.

The chest exam also changes with age. An infant's chest is round. Front-to-back and side-to-side widths are about equal.

table.caption: Normal for age vs. warning signs
rows: Rate in range: infant 30–60, toddler 20–40, preschool 20–35
Rate well above the range for age
Retractions: above the sternum, between ribs, below the sternum
Newborn: irregular breathing, pauses under about 20 seconds
Newborn: blue hands and feet, pink trunk (acrocyanosis)
Central cyanosis: blue lips, tongue, trunk
Grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing, stridor at rest

bullets: Infants: check for pectus carinatum or excavatum. Watch the face and cry during palpation; a grimace can mean tenderness. Feel fremitus while the infant cries.
Newborns: feel near the collarbones for crepitus, which can mean a clavicle broken during a hard delivery.
Toddlers to school age: check for pectus deformities again. No barrel chest after age 6, and no retractions. For fremitus, have the child repeat words or numbers.
sections.example: A 2-year-old with a respiratory infection breathes 32/min while playing. You also see head bobbing, belly breathing, retractions, stridor while calm, and grunting. Act on the head bobbing, retractions, stridor at rest, and grunting. A rate of 32 is in the toddler range. Belly breathing is normal at this age.

check.q: An 8-year-old has a barrel-shaped chest. Expected?
check.a: No. A barrel chest is normal in infants but should not be present after about age 6.

sections.heading: What do you do when a child chokes?
sections.keyIdea: For a conscious choking infant, use back blows and chest thrusts with the head down, never abdominal thrusts.
sections.body:
Foreign objects in the airway are a special risk for young children. If the child can cough hard and cry, air is moving. Encourage coughing and watch closely. Step in only if air stops moving.

If an infant under 1 year can't cry, cough, or breathe, it is an emergency. Do not use abdominal thrusts. The infant's liver is easily injured.
steps: Confirm the infant truly can't cry or cough. Call for help.
Hold the infant face down on your forearm, head lower than chest. Support the head and jaw.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Turn the infant face up, supporting the head, head still lower than the body.
Give up to 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line.
Repeat until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive. Then begin CPR per protocol.
sections.example: A 2-year-old coughed and gagged suddenly while eating trail mix 3 hours ago. No fever. Now the child has an on-and-off cough, wheezing only on the right, and diminished sounds in the right lower lobe. SpO₂ 95%. Suspect an inhaled object in the right bronchus. The child needs imaging and removal, even though they look stable. Teach families to avoid nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, and balloons for toddlers.

sections.heading: How does pregnancy change breathing?
sections.keyIdea: Pregnancy raises the diaphragm and increases breathing, which lowers CO₂ and shrinks the oxygen reserve.
sections.body: Pregnancy changes breathing in ways you can predict. Learn these so you don't mistake them for illness. Then you can spot what is not normal.
bullets: The growing uterus raises the diaphragm, so the lungs can't expand down as far. The ribs flare out, and the chest gets wider.
Breathing rate rises only slightly, about 1–2 breaths a minute. It stays in the normal adult range. A rate well above 20 is not a normal pregnancy change.
Tidal volume and minute ventilation rise. Most extra air comes from deeper breaths.
Residual capacity falls. Less air stays in the lungs after breathing out, so the oxygen reserve is smaller. Ill pregnant clients desaturate fast.
More CO₂ is breathed off, so the pH may be slightly alkaline. A slightly low PaCO₂ is expected.
Nasal lining changes cause stuffiness and nosebleeds. Assess for rhinitis of pregnancy.

table.caption: Expected in pregnancy vs. needs follow-up
rows: Mild shortness of breath on stairs
Slightly alkaline pH, low PaCO₂ (pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 30)
Shortness of breath at rest, chest pain

sections.example: A client at 30 weeks has influenza. She has a stuffy nose, mild breathlessness on stairs, and a small nosebleed. Temp 38.9 °C, RR 28, SpO₂ 93%, fetal heart rate 172. The stuffiness, nosebleed, and breathlessness on stairs are normal. The fever, fast breathing, low SpO₂, and fetal tachycardia need follow-up now.

sections.heading: How do you care for a pregnant client?
sections.keyIdea: Protect two lives: treat the problem fast, avoid lying flat on the back, and check every drug.
sections.body:
The baby depends on the mother's oxygen. So lung problems in pregnancy need prompt care. Your slides list these priorities.

Lying flat on the back lets the heavy uterus press on large blood vessels. Blood flow to the heart and placenta drops. If a pregnant client becomes hypotensive while supine, turn her to her side first.
bullets: Monitor oxygenation during labor to protect the baby's oxygen.
Avoid positions that may harm the fetus, especially lying flat on the back. Side-lying helps.
Treat the underlying problem promptly so mother and baby get enough oxygen.
Involve both the pulmonologist and the obstetrician. Medicine changes are made with both.
Check every medicine before giving it. Some are not safe in pregnancy.
Controlling asthma in pregnancy protects the baby.

check.q: A pregnant client's ABG shows pH 7.44 and PaCO₂ 30. Should you be alarmed?
check.a: No. Deeper breathing in pregnancy lowers CO₂ and makes pH slightly alkaline. Pregnancy lowers CO₂, not O₂.

sections.heading: Older adults: what changes with age?
sections.keyIdea: In older adults, pneumonia may show up as new confusion, weakness, and fast HR and RR, with no fever.
sections.body:
With age, the body's defenses weaken. These changes raise the risk of pneumonia (PNA). Warning signs are often quiet.

Pneumonia in older adults may not cause a fever. Instead, look for confusion, weakness, poor appetite, and faster heart and breathing rates. Sudden confusion is a hypoxia clue until oxygen has been checked. Rule out pneumonia before blaming dementia.
bullets: More respiratory infections
More sleep apnea
Weaker cough reflex, so more choking
More GERD, so more aspiration

table.caption: Assessing the older adult
rows: Crackles at the bases that clear with coughing
Crackles in one area that don't clear, with diminished sounds
Faster heart rate and breathing rate

sections.example: An 82-year-old, usually oriented ×3, is now oriented to person only. New weakness and poor appetite for 2 days. Temp 37.2 °C, HR 112, RR 28, SpO₂ 89%. Mild kyphosis and crackles at both bases that clear with coughing are age-related. Crackles that don't clear in the right lower lobe, plus the other new signs, point to pneumonia, possibly from aspiration.

sections.heading: Caring for and teaching the older adult
sections.keyIdea: Clear secretions, keep lungs expanded, and prevent aspiration by staying upright during and after meals.
sections.body:
Watch for changes in medicines, fluids and nutrition, and thinking. Any of these can be an early clue to an oxygen problem or make one worse.

Your slides say vesicular sounds with a longer breathing-in phase may reflect an obstructive problem, such as COPD or asthma. Many textbooks say obstruction lengthens breathing out instead. Follow your course materials. The main idea is the same: a change in the normal sound pattern needs a closer look.

If a client keeps being readmitted, assess barriers before you teach. Cost, memory, and inhaler technique are common ones.
bullets: Suction more often if needed, since gag and cough reflexes are weaker.
Teach better coughing: slow, deep breaths before a strong cough.
Use incentive spirometry to keep lungs expanded.
Health promotion: quit smoking and stay active.
Check adherence to the treatment plan and barriers to it.
Aspiration precautions: sit upright to eat and stay upright after meals. Raise the head of the bed at night. Take small bites. Don't talk while chewing. Report coughing or choking.

check.q: An 80-year-old with GERD says, "I'll lie down for a nap right after lunch." Does this need teaching?
check.a: Yes. Lying down right after eating increases reflux and aspiration risk. Stay upright after meals.

sections.heading: Genetics, sex, and health promotion
sections.keyIdea: Hemoglobin is strongly inherited, women have lower normal values than men, and prevention looks different at each age.
sections.body:
Hemoglobin level has a strong inherited pattern. Family genes greatly affect how much hemoglobin a person has. Hematocrit has a smaller genetic effect.

Women have lower hemoglobin and hematocrit than men. So normal lab ranges differ by sex. Always compare a result to the client's sex-specific range.

Health promotion changes with age. Each group has its own focus.
bullets: Children: avoid secondhand smoke and get the flu vaccine every year.
Older adults: quit smoking and stay physically active.
Pregnant clients: treat any respiratory illness promptly to protect both lives.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Rule out what is normal for the client's age or stage; the new change left over is the priority.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause the most errors. Use the right column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Belly breathing vs. retractions in a child
Belly breathing under 6 is normal. Retractions are distress.
Blue hands and feet in a newborn are normal. Blue lips or trunk are not.
Pauses under about 20 seconds are normal. 20 seconds or more is apnea.
Infant: back blows and chest thrusts. Never abdominal thrusts.
Pregnancy low CO₂ vs. low O₂
Low CO₂ and slightly high pH are normal. SpO₂ under 95% is not.
New confusion with fast HR and RR is pneumonia until proven otherwise, even with no fever.
Base crackles that clear with cough can be age-related. One-area crackles that persist are not.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect "which finding needs action" questions that mix normal age findings with one real warning sign.
sections.body: Common patterns you will see:
bullets: Normal newborn vs. distress findings
Choking infant: correct steps and order
Toddler with a one-sided wheeze after a choking episode
Normal pregnancy changes vs. findings to report
Afebrile older adult with new confusion
steps: Read the stem: "A client at 30 weeks has stuffy nose, mild breathlessness on stairs, RR 28, SpO₂ 93%, and fetal heart rate 172. Which findings need follow-up?"
What is it really asking? Which findings are normal pregnancy changes, and which are not?
Key cues: RR well above 20, SpO₂ under 95%, fetal tachycardia.
Wrong: the stuffy nose is rhinitis of pregnancy. Mild breathlessness on stairs is expected. Choosing them shows you missed the normal changes.
Answer: RR 28, SpO₂ 93%, and fetal heart rate 172 need follow-up now.
Strategy: cross off what is normal for this age or stage first. What remains is your answer.

sections.heading: Worked case: the baby who is choking
sections.keyIdea: An infant who can't cry or cough needs back blows and chest thrusts right away.
sections.body: A 9-month-old is eating a snack. Suddenly the baby can't cry, has blue lips, and is still awake. The parent screams for help.
steps: Notice: no cry, no cough, blue lips, still conscious.
Interpret: complete airway blockage in an infant. This is an emergency.
Act: call for help. Hold the baby face down, head low, and give up to 5 back blows.
Then turn face up, head low, and give up to 5 chest thrusts just below the nipple line.
Repeat until the object comes out. If the baby becomes unresponsive, begin CPR per protocol.

check.q: Why not use abdominal thrusts on this infant?
check.a: An infant's liver is easily injured. Back blows and chest thrusts are used instead.

mnemonics.name: 5 and 5, head down
mnemonics.text: Choking infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, always with the head lower than the chest.

pearls: Belly breathing under 6 is normal; retractions, grunting, head bobbing, and stridor at rest are not.
Choking infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, head down. No abdominal thrusts.
A sudden choking episode plus a one-sided wheeze in a toddler is an inhaled object until proven otherwise, usually on the right.
Pregnancy lowers CO₂, not O₂. SpO₂ under 95% needs follow-up.
Older adult with new confusion and fast HR and RR but no fever: think pneumonia before dementia.
Compare hemoglobin and hematocrit to the client's sex-specific range.
redFlags: Retractions, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing, or stridor at rest in a child: assess and act now.
Infant who can't cry or cough after eating: call for help and start back blows and chest thrusts.
Pregnant client with SpO₂ under 95%, fever, fast breathing, or fetal tachycardia: notify the provider promptly.
Older adult with new confusion, fast heart rate, and fast breathing, even without fever: assess for pneumonia and notify the provider.

checks.q: A 2-hour-old newborn breathes 52/min irregularly with 5–10 second pauses. Hands and feet are blue; the trunk is pink. Normal?
checks.a: Yes. Irregular breathing at 30–60 with short pauses and acrocyanosis are normal. Grunting or flaring would not be.

checks.q: Why do pregnant clients desaturate faster when they get sick?
checks.a: Residual capacity falls, so the oxygen reserve is smaller, while oxygen needs rise.

checks.q: In an 82-year-old, which suggest pneumonia: kyphosis, new confusion, base crackles that clear with cough, HR 112?
checks.a: New confusion and HR 112. Kyphosis and crackles that clear with coughing can be age-related.

checks.q: A toddler is coughing hard and crying after inhaling a piece of food. What do you do?
checks.a: Encourage the child to keep coughing and watch closely. Step in only if air stops moving.

checks.q: A pregnant client lying on her back becomes dizzy with low blood pressure. First action?
checks.a: Turn her onto her side. This takes the uterus off the large blood vessels.
